question: find_peaks, find_targets or match_features returns too many peaks or features
answer: The result depends on the dataset. Usually raising `min_snr` (default 2) or `min_intensity` (default 500) is enough to drop small peaks mixed with the `noise`. You can also set `min_integral` (off by default) to drop peaks with a small area, or raise `min_peak_width_points` (default 3) to drop narrow peaks with few scans. Check the `noise` level with `find_noise_level` and set `min_intensity` above it. If the automatic `noise` estimate is off, turn `auto_noise` off and set `noise` to that value. In `get_peak`, `find_targets`, `find_transitions`, `find_features` and `match_features`, set these inside the `find_peaks` option.

question: find_peaks, find_targets or match_features returns too few peaks or features
answer: Too few peaks or features usually means `min_intensity` (default 500) or `min_snr` (default 2) is too high for your data. If your peaks are above `min_intensity` but still missing, the `noise` estimate may be too high, for example when the run has washing cycles, so `min_snr` × `noise` drops real peaks. Check the `noise` with `find_noise_level`. If it is too high, turn `auto_noise` off and set `noise` to a value that fits your chromatogram, or lower `min_snr`. If that doesn’t fix it, lower `min_peak_width_points` (default 3), because it drops narrow peaks with few scans. In `get_peak`, `find_targets`, `find_transitions`, `find_features` and `match_features`, set these inside the `find_peaks` option.

question: find_targets picks the wrong peak for some compounds
answer: This usually means the target `rt` or `range` does not fit your data. The peak is searched only inside `rt` ± `range`, so if `rt` is off or `range` is too narrow, the right peak is missed or a neighbour peak is picked. The best way to set them is from your own samples. Use the median retention time of the compound as `rt`, and its standard deviation to set `range`. Retention times shift less within one batch or plate, so values from the same batch work well. If you process several batches at the same time, a warp model is the better choice, see `predict_rts`.
intro: This usually means the target `rt` or `range` does not fit your data. The peak is searched only inside `rt` ± `range`, so if `rt` is off or `range` is too narrow, the right peak is missed or a neighbour peak is picked.

If you process several batches at the same time, a warp model is the better choice, see `predict_rts`.

notes.get_peak: In `get_peak`, `range` 0 searches the whole trace, so set `range` to stay near `rt`.

question: find_peaks, get_peak, find_targets, find_transitions, find_features or match_features returns nothing
answer: An empty result usually means the peak detection is running on chromatograms that are empty. Display the chromatogram from `calculate_eic` to see whether it is empty. Check the units, a wrong `time_unit` with `from` and `to` can read only a few seconds. A very short window between `from` and `to`, under a minute, can also cut the peak off, so widen it if the peak may be near its edges. If the chromatogram shows the peak, it may be below `min_intensity` (default 500) or `min_snr` (default 2), so lower them, inside the `find_peaks` option when the function has one. A noise estimate that is too high, for example when the run has washing cycles, makes `min_snr` × noise drop every peak. Check the noise with `find_noise_level`. If it is too high, turn `auto_noise` off and set noise to a value that fits your chromatogram.

question: find_targets finds most peaks but misses some of them
answer: Retention times can shift a little between runs. When a peak moves out of the search window, it is missed even if it is in the data. For larger shifts, or when you process several batches at the same time, a warp model is the better choice. Train it with PyTorch to learn the flow in your LC, export it to ONNX, and open it with `load_model` and `load_warp`. `calibrate` learns the shift from a few anchor samples, like LTRs or QCs, and `predict_rts` gives the expected rt of each target in each sample.
intro: Retention times can shift a little between runs. When a peak moves out of the search window, it is missed even if it is in the data.

question: reading a remote .ion file is slow
answer: A query reads only the parts of the file it needs. When you write the file, a smaller `mz_window` (default 20 Da) and a smaller `block_size` (default 8 MB) let each query read less. With `mz_window` 0 each spectrum is kept whole, so queries read more.

question: find_noise_level gives a noise level that is too low or too high
answer: The noise level depends on the part of the chromatogram you give to `find_noise_level`. A noise level that is too low means that part is probably not representative of the run, for example the peak is not there or the zone is mostly empty. A noise level that is too high means that zone or the whole chromatogram has problem zones, like a washing cycle or solvent spikes, that make the noise hard to estimate. Plot the chromatogram from `calculate_eic` and check which zones are empty or complex. Then calculate the EIC again with `from` and `to` set to leave those zones out. To get the noise level, use an EIC from a zone that looks right.
